title: Embassy officials secretly entered home of Canadian employee, investigator finds
html:
Global Affairs Canada's headquarters at the Lester B. Pearson Building on Sussex Drive in Ottawa.Justin Tang/The Globe and Mail

A federally appointed investigator has recommended that Global Affairs Canada take steps to protect the privacy of Canadian diplomats after an employee’s home was entered without her knowledge.

The entry, authorized by federal officials, was not disclosed to the employee for two weeks. She said the intrusion triggered feelings of fear, anxiety, humiliation, degradation and psychological distress − all reasonable responses under the circumstances, investigator Albert Bissonnette said.

Mr. Bissonnette, of ProActive Security, was hired by Global Affairs after a labour program representative recommended an investigation under the harassment and workplace violence sections of the Canada Labour Code.

The case involved “unannounced entry into an employee’s personal residence, followed by a prolonged failure to disclose that entry and an initial denial,” Mr. Bissonnette wrote in a 27-page report, submitted to Global Affairs in June.

This could “reasonably be expected to cause offence, humiliation, and psychological injury” under those circumstances, he said, concluding that the incident met the definition of harassment and workplace violence under the labour code.

An employee’s privacy in their home, he said, is “sacrosanct and must be respected to the extent possible.”

Global Affairs says it is “carefully reviewing” the report’s recommendations. “As part of this review, the Department will consider opportunities and measures to strengthen its policies, procedures and practices,” department spokesperson Rachael Dolan told The Globe and Mail.

For privacy and confidentiality reasons, the department said it cannot provide any further information about the case.

The employee is not named in the report. But The Globe has established that it was Jennifer Boudreau, a former executive assistant in the Canadian embassy in Zimbabwe, who went public with her complaint in 2024 when she filed a report at a Zimbabwean police station, alleging “unlawful entry in aggravating circumstances.” The police disclosed her allegation in a public report at the time.

Ms. Boudreau, a Canadian who was an 18-year employee of Global Affairs, said an embassy official entered her bedroom in December 2023 to obtain video footage from a closed-circuit camera system that monitored her property, in connection with a separate administrative investigation. When she returned home later that day, she noticed an open wardrobe door in her bedroom, which led her to suspect the entry.

Mr. Bissonnette, who reviewed more than 4,000 pages of documents in his probe, found that the embassy official and a technician had used a duplicate key to enter the employee’s home without her knowledge or consent. When the employee repeatedly asked about the incident, officials insisted falsely that the entry had not occurred.

Ms. Boudreau was dismissed from Global Affairs in January 2025. She says the department alleged she had been insubordinate and disrespectful. She is fighting the dismissal.

In an interview, she said the investigator’s report is evidence that she deserves an apology and should be reinstated.

Mr. Bissonnette, in his report, said the entry into an employee’s home without their knowledge was “inherently intrusive” and would be felt as a “significant violation of their personal space and privacy” by any reasonable person.

“An employee’s residence, even when government-owned, constitutes the employee’s personal home during the period of their assignment,” he said. “It is the space in which an employee’s private life is conducted, and in which a reasonable expectation of privacy ordinarily exists.”

He recommended that Global Affairs reassess its tenant agreements and consider adding a clause to describe the circumstances in which a tenant should be told about an entry to their home, if the tenant did not specifically approve the entry.

He also recommended that Global Affairs develop a policy on the authorizations that are required before an employee’s home can be entered. And he recommended that, before any entry of a home, the department should assess whether the entry could be done in the presence of the employee or with prior notice.
summary: Report says incident met the definition of harassment and workplace violence under the labour code
